edition.deck: The latest developments in a consequential US election, renewed strikes in Ukraine and decisions affecting communities in Britain and Denmark.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises overnight developments and fresh reporting. Returning subjects are included only where the gather adds a material development or new evidence.

content.headline: Nine people killed as business jet crashes into Florida neighbourhood
content.shortHeadline: Nine killed in Florida business jet crash
content.standfirst: The Learjet crashed into a residential area near Palm Beach, killing everyone on board. Authorities said nearby residents were evacuated as investigators began examining what happened.

image.caption: Emergency vehicles at the scene of the Florida plane crash.

sources.originalTitle: 'Like a missile coming down' - Nine killed in fiery Florida jet crash

segments.body: The Learjet 60 crashed in Cresthaven, Florida, on Sunday, killing all nine people aboard, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. The aircraft had taken off from Austin, Texas, and was travelling to the Bahamas. The cause of the crash has not been established.

segments.title: Investigation and disruption
segments.body: Local officials said about 600 residents of a nearby trailer-park community were evacuated. The impact damaged infrastructure, including water lines, and officials said the road would remain closed for at least 30 days. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating with support from the Federal Aviation Administration.

content.headline: Ukraine resumes refinery strikes as Russian attacks cut power to homes
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine resumes Russian refinery strikes as power outages spread
content.standfirst: Ukraine says it has resumed attacks on Russian oil facilities while Russian strikes damaged energy infrastructure across four Ukrainian regions. The local truce that enabled evacuations from Oleshky has also ended.

image.caption: A fire at a Russian refinery after a reported Ukrainian drone strike.

sources.originalTitle: Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries
Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv says air raid warning app likely hacked after users receive false alerts
Spectacular photos show Russian oil plants burn as Trump truce collapses
Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as Kherson ceasefire ends

segments.body: Russian state media reported Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries in Nizhny Novgorod and Samara regions. Kyiv has not confirmed the refinery attacks, but President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine struck a defence-industry site in Russia’s Rostov region. The Guardian reports the renewed refinery strikes follow pressure from Washington to pause them.

segments.title: Energy and evacuation
segments.body: Zelensky said Russian strikes hit energy infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions, leaving hundreds of thousands of households without power; repairs continued as emergency cuts affected the country. A six-day local ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky ended on Sunday, after residents were able to evacuate. Ukrainian observers said Russian forces used the pause to reinforce positions.

content.headline: Michigan Senate race jolted as Democrat endorses Republican rival
content.shortHeadline: Democrat’s last-minute endorsement jolts Michigan Senate race
content.standfirst: Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic nomination to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers two days before the vote. The move has intensified party divisions in a closely watched Senate contest.

image.caption: Haley Stevens and Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers at a church service in Detroit.

sources.originalTitle: Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Abdul El-Sayed’s Republican rival Mike Rogers
Democrat endorses Republican candidate in key Michigan Senate race as party spat erupts
Democrats rocked by ‘despicable betrayal’ on eve of midterms vote
Democrat infighting over Israel could hand Trump election victory
Trump launches racist diatribe against Abdul El-Sayed at Iowa rally
Democrats have high hopes for midterms, but polls have let them down before

segments.body: Stevens appeared with Rogers at a Detroit church on Sunday and announced her endorsement, saying El-Sayed had made clear she was unwelcome in his campaign. The rupture followed a dispute over an advert linking US support for Israel with rising prices; El-Sayed said he opposed the advert and had no involvement in it.

segments.title: A race with national stakes
segments.body: Democratic leaders condemned Stevens’s decision, and several members of her staff reportedly resigned. Donald Trump praised her and attacked El-Sayed, a Muslim, with anti-Muslim language at an Iowa rally. The Michigan contest is among the close Senate races that could help determine control of Congress; polling does not guarantee the result.

content.headline: Binance reopens after record hack as customers withdraw $3.6bn
content.shortHeadline: Binance customers withdraw $3.6bn after record hack
content.standfirst: The cryptocurrency exchange processed a large net outflow after reopening withdrawals following a hack that affected $6.3bn in digital assets. Binance says it has covered about 95% of the stolen funds and will meet the remaining loss.

sources.originalTitle: Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after record crypto hack

segments.body: Binance said it processed $4.649bn in withdrawals and $1.01bn in deposits on Sunday, a net outflow of about $3.64bn. It said an initial surge later eased and that withdrawals for major cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin and Ethereum, had resumed as security checks continued.

segments.title: Recovery and attribution
segments.body: The exchange said it had replaced about 95% of the assets stolen in the breach, while promising to cover the full financial impact. The FBI attributed the attack to the North Korean-linked group TraderTraitor and published wallet addresses it said were connected to the group. The cause of the breach remains under investigation; Binance said early checks pointed to an engineer’s compromised laptop.

content.headline: Israeli strikes kill eight in Gaza despite ceasefire, hospitals say
content.shortHeadline: Eight reported killed in Gaza strikes despite ceasefire
content.standfirst: Hospitals and Gaza authorities report that eight people, including a four-year-old boy, were killed in strikes in Gaza City and Khan Younis. Israel said it struck what it described as military operatives but has not provided further details.

image.caption: Mourners attend a funeral for Palestinians killed in an Israeli strike.

sources.originalTitle: Israeli strikes in Gaza kill eight including child, hospitals say
Otte dræbt i israelske angreb i Gaza

segments.body: Hospital officials said three people, including a child, were killed in a strike near Cairo School in Gaza City. Gaza’s Hamas-run interior ministry said five police officers were killed in a drone attack in Khan Younis. The Israeli military said it had carried out two attacks on what it described as military operatives.

segments.title: Ceasefire and wider toll
segments.body: The reported deaths come despite a ceasefire that began last October. Israeli strikes have continued, and Gaza’s Hamas-run health ministry says 1,580 people have been killed since the truce began; the UN considers the ministry’s figures reliable. A US-brokered peace plan has stalled.

content.headline: Scientists warn temporary overshoot of 1.5C could cause lasting ice loss
content.shortHeadline: Scientists warn climate overshoot could cause lasting ice loss
content.standfirst: A report by 80 scientists says glacier and polar-ice damage could persist even if global temperatures later fall back to the Paris target. The authors call for any overshoot to be as brief as possible.

image.caption: Ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica are melting faster than in the 1990s, the report says.

sources.originalTitle: Cryosphere faces permanent damage when world overshoots 1.5C, scientists warn

segments.body: The report, compiled by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the UN Environment Programme, says warming above 1.5C risks long-lasting losses of glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. The scientists say much of the damage would remain even if temperatures were later brought back down.

segments.title: Risks under current policies
segments.body: Under current policies, the report estimates warming could reach about 2.8C, with severe consequences for ice-dependent regions and water supplies. It says a higher overshoot could thaw nearly all near-surface permafrost and increase the likelihood of major disruption to ocean circulation. A climate scientist not involved in the report said the losses would carry worldwide consequences.

content.headline: Qatar seeks deal to reopen Hormuz as US-Iran talks continue
content.shortHeadline: Qatar mediates as US-Iran talks seek to reopen Hormuz
content.standfirst: Indirect talks in Doha have continued for a third day, with Qatar trying to link the release of Iranian assets to reopening the strait and restarting nuclear negotiations. No agreement has been announced.

image.caption: A mural in Tehran as Iran’s foreign minister calls for diplomacy with the US.

sources.originalTitle: Negotiators ‘braced for worst’ over US-Iran talks to reopen strait of Hormuz

segments.body: Qatar is mediating between Washington and Tehran on a proposal involving more than $6bn in Iranian assets and reopening the strait of Hormuz. Iran has said it could reopen the waterway within two days of US action on the blockade, sanctions and frozen assets; it has not agreed to discuss its nuclear programme.

segments.title: An uncertain path
segments.body: Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he hoped Washington would choose diplomacy, while the US has said it is open to a diplomatic solution. Negotiations are taking place amid warnings of further escalation and a recent missile strike on a Qatari LNG tanker. Gulf officials say they are prepared for the risk of renewed conflict.

content.headline: French prosecutors open attempted-murder inquiry after petrol bomb attack
content.shortHeadline: France probes petrol-bomb attack on police as protests continue
content.standfirst: An officer was burned during clashes in Paris, prompting prosecutors to open an attempted-murder investigation. The Interior Ministry reported more than 770 arrests during the latest weekend of demonstrations.

sources.originalTitle: France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police

segments.body: French prosecutors have opened an attempted-murder investigation after an incendiary device was thrown at police in Paris. The officer suffered burns to an ankle and minor hand injuries. Police said no one had been arrested for the attack at the time of the report.

segments.title: Protests and injuries
segments.body: The Interior Ministry said more than 770 people were arrested as demonstrations over living costs and public services continued for a third weekend. The protests were largely peaceful, though police used tear gas in some cities. Organisers have also reported serious injuries among demonstrators in recent weeks.

content.headline: UK expected to ease settlement rules for care workers already here
content.shortHeadline: Care workers may be spared a 15-year wait to settle in UK
content.standfirst: The Home Secretary is expected to set out revised settlement rules on Monday. Reports say care workers already in Britain may be exempt from the longest proposed wait, while campaigners warn the changes could affect staffing and migrants’ settled expectations.

image.caption: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is expected to announce revised settlement rules.

sources.originalTitle: Home secretary to make some migrants wait 10 years or more for right to settle in UK
Carers set to be spared in migrant crackdown as overseas recruits plunge by 90%

segments.body: Shabana Mahmood is expected to announce reforms that would usually double the qualifying period for settlement from five to 10 years. Under the original proposal, some workers, including care workers, could wait 15 years. The Guardian reports ministers are considering an exemption for care workers already in the UK; the final rules have not yet been confirmed.

segments.title: Workforce concerns
segments.body: The King’s Fund analysis reported by the i Paper says overseas care-worker recruitment has fallen from a peak of 105,000 in 2023–24 and could reach 10,000 in 2026–27 if current trends continue. It also says new British starters are falling, while more workers left than joined last year. The Home Office declined to comment ahead of the announcement.

perspectives.body: The i Paper adds workforce figures from the King’s Fund, highlighting that international recruitment is declining while demand for care is forecast to grow.

content.headline: UK may trade student-fee concessions for access to EU industry scheme
content.shortHeadline: UK weighs EU student-fee deal for industrial-scheme access
content.standfirst: As the UK and EU negotiate a package for their 20 November summit, ministers are weighing cheaper tuition for EU students against access to the bloc’s proposed industrial programme. Negotiations over youth mobility also remain unresolved.

image.caption: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is due to host Andy Burnham in Brussels.

sources.originalTitle: UK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe scheme
UK may have to accept almost 100,000 young Europeans a year to unlock Brexit deal

segments.body: The UK is prepared to consider charging EU students domestic-level tuition, but only if British firms gain access to the EU’s proposed Made in Europe industrial scheme, the Guardian reports. Treasury estimates put the possible annual cost as high as £450m under one scenario; a government official described that figure as speculative.

segments.title: Other parts of the package
segments.body: The summit talks also cover food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. The i Paper reports the UK is considering an annual cap nearer 100,000 young Europeans, while EU negotiators have pushed for that level. The final number and the wider package remain under negotiation.

content.headline: Security experts warn Chinese electric buses could be remotely disabled
content.shortHeadline: Experts warn of remote-access risks in Chinese electric buses
content.standfirst: UK councils have bought hundreds of Yutong electric buses, whose internet-connected SIM cards are used for software updates. Security specialists warn remote access could pose a risk, while the government and manufacturer dispute that passengers face a danger.

image.caption: Yutong electric buses, some of which are already operating in Britain.

sources.originalTitle: The electric buses that China can stop in the road – coming to a town near you

segments.body: The i Paper reports that about 640 Yutong buses are operating in England, with more planned in Scotland. Security specialists say the internet-connected systems used for software updates could potentially be used to disable vehicles. The National Cyber Security Centre has said remote stopping is technically possible.

segments.title: Government and company response
segments.body: The government says the buses operate safely and that there is no cause for passenger concern. Yutong says its internet-enabled software is not connected to the vehicles’ main driving controls. The report says Norway’s public transport company introduced additional security measures after investigating its own Yutong fleet.

content.headline: Experts raise concern over bird flu outbreak on Utah mink farm
content.shortHeadline: Mink farm bird flu outbreak prompts pandemic-preparedness concerns
content.standfirst: Scientists say infection among farmed mink could give bird flu opportunities to change, though the virus is not currently spreading easily between people. The report also examines how the UK would detect and respond to a new strain.

image.caption: Mink on fur farms may provide conditions for bird flu to change, scientists warn.

sources.originalTitle: Bird flu is one mutation from serious risk to humans – how prepared is the UK?

segments.body: An outbreak of bird flu among mink on a Utah fur farm has worried scientists because mink respiratory systems are similar to humans’ and the animals can carry different flu strains. Researchers say the viruses could exchange genetic material, but the report does not say a strain capable of sustained human transmission has emerged.

segments.title: UK readiness
segments.body: The UK Health Security Agency said it has systems to detect human cases and is ready to respond. The report notes that standard vaccines could take about six months to produce for a new strain, while an mRNA vaccine could potentially be made faster. One expert called for researchers to test whether bird-flu tests could be developed within 30 days.

content.headline: Tommy Robinson conviction leaves anti-migrant movement without clear successor
content.shortHeadline: Robinson conviction leaves far right facing a leadership gap
content.standfirst: The far-right activist was found guilty of harassing two journalists, with sentencing due in December. Analysts say his possible imprisonment and the separate custody of a potential successor could leave the anti-migrant movement without a prominent leader.

image.caption: Tommy Robinson and supporters outside Southwark Crown Court.

sources.originalTitle: Tommy Robinson conviction leaves far right with leadership void

segments.body: A jury found Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, guilty of harassment causing fear of violence to two Daily Mail journalists. Evidence included threats and the use of an investigator, the Guardian reports. Robinson will be sentenced on 16 December and could face up to 10 years, though the eventual sentence is not yet known.

segments.title: Movement in flux
segments.body: Hope Not Hate researcher Joe Mulhall said there is no obvious replacement for Robinson, while Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, is in custody ahead of a trial over an alleged attack on a dinghy; he denies wrongdoing. The report says the movement is fragmented, and that the conviction may complicate efforts by politicians to court its supporters.

content.headline: London residents left without heating after energy debt emerges
content.shortHeadline: More than 120 London flats lose gas over historic debt
content.standfirst: Residents at a north-west London development say they lost hot water and heating despite paying monthly energy charges. The management company says it is working with the freeholder and supplier to restore gas while it reviews the disputed debt.

image.caption: Residents at Middle Yard have been left without hot water after the gas supply was cut.

sources.originalTitle: The leasehold flats left with no hot water or heating over mystery £600,000 bill

segments.body: More than 120 apartments at Middle Yard in Dollis Hill have been without gas since Friday, leaving residents without hot water or heating. Residents say they paid their bills through a management company but were later told that about £600,000 in historic gas and electricity debts remained unpaid.

segments.title: Responsibility unresolved
segments.body: The current management company says it was unaware of the full extent of the debt when it took over in May and is urgently working with the freeholder and energy supplier. It says it is reviewing how energy costs were budgeted and recovered, and that it is too early to say who is responsible for the shortfall or what residents may ultimately owe.

content.headline: Poll finds 48% of Britons favour rejoining the European Union
content.shortHeadline: Poll puts support for UK rejoining EU at 48%
content.standfirst: A BMG poll for the i Paper found 48% would back rejoining the EU and 35% would prefer to stay out. The figures come as the government signals closer ties, but do not show how opinion would respond to a full campaign.

image.caption: The poll comes amid renewed calls for closer links between the UK and the EU.

sources.originalTitle: The numbers that show how support for reversing Brexit is creeping up

segments.body: The survey of 1,529 adults in Great Britain found support for rejoining had risen three points since the previous month, while support for staying out had fallen by three. Seventeen per cent said they did not know. The poll was conducted on 28 and 29 October.

segments.title: Debate ahead
segments.body: The pollster said much of the pro-rejoin lead came from people who did not vote in the 2016 referendum or were too young to vote. The government has not committed to rejoining; the report says the Prime Minister has ruled out a return to freedom of movement without a referendum, while the shape of any closer relationship remains uncertain.

content.headline: TV 2 confirms reused audio as it investigates withdrawn programme
content.shortHeadline: TV 2 confirms audio was reused in withdrawn show
content.standfirst: The broadcaster says a laugh was used twice in “Alle elsker Rasmus” and has opened an internal review after withdrawing the programme. Two sound experts told DR their analyses found a strong match between the recordings.

image.caption: TV 2 says it made mistakes in “Alle elsker Rasmus” and confirms that audio was reused.

sources.originalTitle: TV 2 bekræfter, at lydklip er blevet genbrugt i central scene i udskældt program

segments.body: TV 2 says an audio clip was reused in a central scene of “Alle elsker Rasmus”, the programme it withdrew after criticism of its treatment of comedian Rasmus Wallbridge. Content director Ulla Pors said the reuse should not have happened and that the broadcaster was investigating the production and its decisions.

segments.title: Expert analysis and criticism
segments.body: Two audio experts consulted by DR found substantial similarity between the two laughs; one said it was the same sequence placed at different points in the episode. A media-law lecturer told DR that editing alone is not necessarily a press-ethics violation, but that the effect on the person portrayed matters.

content.headline: DR traces Danish tax-fraud claims to Arizona property and cigarette firm
content.shortHeadline: DR links Arizona properties to Danish tax-fraud recovery case
content.standfirst: Danish authorities allege that an Arizona company received money connected to the dividend-tax fraud case and used it to buy property. The company denies knowingly handling fraud proceeds, and the court case is ongoing.

image.caption: Cigarette packs marketed on Emerald Industries’ website.

sources.originalTitle: Afsløring: Dansk milliardjagt fører til mystisk amerikansk cigaretfirma

segments.body: DR reports that Danish authorities are seeking control of Arizona properties or compensation of up to $22m from Emerald Industries. They allege funds linked to the fraud for which Sanjay Shah was convicted passed through companies in Dubai before reaching Emerald. The company denies knowingly receiving or handling proceeds of fraud.

segments.title: Questions still before the court
segments.body: DR’s review found property purchases and company records, but says it could not independently identify retailers or production sites for Emerald’s cigarette brands. The company says it received legitimate payments for cigarette sales and disputes the Dubai court’s jurisdiction. The case has not been decided, and the Danish tax authority did not respond to DR’s questions before publication.

content.headline: US says Greenland agreement protects security but does not resolve Trump’s claim
content.shortHeadline: Rubio backs Greenland agreement as questions over Trump’s claims stay
content.standfirst: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the agreement with Denmark and Greenland protects US and allied security. He did not directly explain why Donald Trump continues to describe Greenland as American, leaving the dispute over the deal’s meaning unresolved.

image.caption: Marco Rubio speaks about the agreement involving Greenland, Denmark and the United States.

sources.originalTitle: Har Trump eller Danmark og Grønland misforstået aftalen?

segments.body: Asked by DR whether Trump had misunderstood the agreement or Denmark and Greenland had, Rubio said the president was informed and supported it. He described it as a security agreement that protects US and NATO interests, including access to Greenland, whether the territory becomes independent or remains part of Denmark.

segments.title: What remains unclear
segments.body: Rubio did not directly address Trump’s repeated statements implying that Greenland belongs to the United States. Danish and Greenlandic politicians have said the agreement transferred no sovereignty or ownership. DR’s reporter said Rubio’s comments did not explain the difference between those positions and the president’s public claims.

content.headline: Copenhagen hotels report losses over Turkish bookings that go unused
content.shortHeadline: Copenhagen hotels report losses from unused Turkish bookings
content.standfirst: Hoteliers say a growing number of reservations from Turkey are cancelled late or go unused, costing the sector millions. They suspect some bookings may support visa applications, but the purpose of the reservations has not been established.

image.caption: A Copenhagen hotel amid reports of a rise in unused bookings.

sources.originalTitle: Mystiske hotelaflysninger vækker mistanke om "visumshopping"

segments.body: HORESTA says nine in 10 Copenhagen hotels it surveyed reported unusually high no-shows on bookings from Turkey. The hotels say the pattern has increased over two to three years and has caused substantial losses. Denmark received 44,582 Turkish visa applications in 2025, up from 10,727 in 2024, according to figures cited by TV 2.

segments.title: Visa-shopping suspicion unconfirmed
segments.body: Some hoteliers suspect reservations are made to support applications for Danish Schengen visas and cancelled after a visa is granted, with travel intended elsewhere in the Schengen area. The Danish embassy in Ankara has previously warned applicants against visa-shopping. The Foreign Ministry had not responded to TV 2’s questions about the reported pattern by publication.

content.headline: Arsenal end 14-year Anfield wait and move three points clear
content.shortHeadline: Arsenal end Anfield drought to go three clear
content.standfirst: Kai Havertz’s goal gives Arsenal their first Premier League win at Liverpool since 2012. The victory, four days after their cup defeat by Fleetwood, puts them three points clear at the top.

image.caption: Arsenal move clear at the top after a rare win at Liverpool.

sources.originalTitle: From Fleetwood embarrassment to 'magical' Anfield win 14 years in making
I'll tell my players to dive in future - Iraola

segments.body: Arsenal held on for a 1-0 win at Anfield, where they had not won a Premier League match since 2012. Kai Havertz scored in the first half, and Arsenal’s defence kept Liverpool without a shot on target in the second. The result leaves Arsenal three points clear after nine games.

segments.title: The penalty debate
segments.body: Liverpool were denied a penalty after Jurrien Timber pulled Alexander Isak’s shirt as the striker went for a header. Isak stayed on his feet and did not appeal; VAR judged the tug too slight to overturn the decision. Former assistant referee Darren Cann said it was close to the line and could have been given on another day.

perspectives.body: Bournemouth manager Andoni Iraola said he would tell Isak to go down in future, arguing that players who stay on their feet will not get such decisions. He also described Isak as honest.

content.headline: Hibs beat Hearts to reach League Cup final after late scare
content.shortHeadline: Hibs beat Hearts to reach League Cup final
content.standfirst: Hibernian held on for a 2-1 win in the Edinburgh derby semi-final at Hampden, despite a late chance for Hearts. They will face Rangers in the final.

sources.originalTitle: Giant curiosity Hibs finally liberated from the sucker punch

segments.body: Hibs came from behind to beat Hearts 2-1 and reach the Scottish League Cup final, where they will meet Rangers. Hearts had a late opportunity to force extra time, but Claudio Braga missed from close range. Hibs celebrated their first victory over their city rivals at Hampden.

segments.title: A possible turning point
segments.body: The win came during a difficult run for Hibs: they had no league wins in six and had scored only four goals in their previous six matches. Their performance improved after conceding early, but they now need to carry that resilience into the league, where they are bottom of the Premiership.

content.headline: Harriet Dart wins first WTA title after breakthrough week in Guangzhou
content.shortHeadline: Dart wins first WTA title in Guangzhou
content.standfirst: The 30-year-old beat Austrian teenager Lilli Tagger to claim her first WTA title. Dart credits coach Marion Bartoli’s belief with helping her regain confidence after falling outside the world’s top 100.

image.caption: Harriet Dart after winning her first WTA title.

sources.originalTitle: How Dart revived career with help of Wimbledon champion

segments.body: Harriet Dart won the Guangzhou Open by beating Lilli Tagger, completing the best week of her career with her first WTA title. She is projected to rise from 115th to 83rd in Monday’s rankings. Dart has won 19 of her 24 tour-level matches on hard courts since Wimbledon.

segments.title: A partnership built on belief
segments.body: Dart has worked part-time with 2013 Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli since the start of the season. Dart said Bartoli’s belief had helped her believe more in herself; Britain captain Anne Keothavong also noted greater confidence as Dart fought back from behind in Guangzhou.

content.headline: Alcaraz beats De Minaur to win Vienna and extend ATP 500 run
content.shortHeadline: Alcaraz beats De Minaur to win Vienna
content.standfirst: Carlos Alcaraz beat Alex de Minaur 6-1 6-4 in the Vienna final, extending his winning run at ATP 500 events to 26 matches. He has won all 16 of his matches at that level in 2026.

image.caption: Carlos Alcaraz wins a rally at the Vienna Open.

sources.originalTitle: Alcaraz wins Vienna Open to maintain perfect record

segments.body: Alcaraz needed 87 minutes to beat De Minaur and win the Vienna Open. The Spaniard broke serve three times in the first set and sealed the second with a forehand winner. It was his seventh win in seven meetings with the Australian.

content.headline: Almgren wins New York Marathon on debut as Chepkirui takes women’s race
content.shortHeadline: Almgren wins New York Marathon on debut
content.standfirst: Sweden’s Andreas Almgren won the men’s race in 2:06:01, becoming the first European-born man to take the New York title in 30 years. Sheila Chepkirui won the women’s race by six seconds.

image.caption: Andreas Almgren, winner of the New York Marathon on his debut.

sources.originalTitle: Almgren wins in New York on marathon debut

segments.body: Andreas Almgren won the New York Marathon on his debut, finishing in 2:06:01 and 13 seconds ahead of Italy’s Yemaneberhan Crippa. The 31-year-old’s year already includes European 10,000m gold and a European half-marathon record.

segments.title: Chepkirui edges the women’s race
segments.body: Kenya’s Sheila Chepkirui claimed her second New York Marathon victory in 2:24:36, six seconds ahead of American Jessica McClain. Hellen Obiri finished one second further back in third.

content.headline: Man City beat London City, but Lionesses show European ambitions
content.shortHeadline: London City impress in defeat by Man City
content.standfirst: Manchester City won 2-1 despite London City Lionesses having 24 shots. The performance strengthened the case that the newly promoted side could challenge for European football, though consistency and ownership rules remain questions.

image.caption: Manchester City edge London City Lionesses in a WSL thriller.

sources.originalTitle: Defeat for London City - but is Europe a real possibility?

segments.body: Khadija Shaw and Lauren Hemp scored as Manchester City won 2-1 at London City Lionesses, continuing their lead at the top of the Women’s Super League. London City had 24 shots, six on target, but could not convert their pressure into a result.

segments.title: The European question
segments.body: London City’s performance has made their Champions League ambitions look less remote, but the club still has work to do and results have not always matched its performances. UEFA rules on multi-club ownership could also become an issue if both London City and Michele Kang’s Lyon qualify for the same competition.

perspectives.body: Chief executive Martin Semmens said the club wants to compete in Europe and believes there may be structured ways to do so while respecting the rules. He said the squad is still developing.

content.headline: RFL sets up long-term review after England World Cup exits
content.shortHeadline: RFL plans review after England World Cup exits
content.standfirst: England’s men and women both exited their Rugby League World Cups in the group stage. The Rugby Football League has appointed a panel to examine the game’s future, while warning that change will take years.

sources.originalTitle: The plan England's rugby league bosses hope avoids repeat of World Cup pain

segments.body: The Rugby Football League has set up a panel to plan the future of the English game after both England teams left their World Cups at the group stage. Former Great Britain captain Paul Sculthorpe, retiring England women’s captain Jodie Cunningham and Adrian Morley are among those involved.

segments.title: A long-term challenge
segments.body: The review is intended to cover player development, the domestic game and how rugby league attracts audiences. RFL chief executive Ian Nolan acknowledged factors including travel and tournament format, but said they could not be used as excuses. The report says the women’s domestic competition is effectively amateur while their World Cup opponents include professionals.

content.headline: 14-year-old hands himself in as police investigate Lowery video
content.shortHeadline: Police investigate video after 14-year-old hands himself in
content.standfirst: West Midlands Police say a 14-year-old has handed himself in after a video appeared to show a supporter taunting Sunderland fans with a photograph of Bradley Lowery, who died aged six from cancer. The investigation is ongoing.

sources.originalTitle: Boy, 14, hands himself in to police over Bradley Lowery video

segments.body: West Midlands Police have launched an investigation into a video that appeared to show a supporter taunting Sunderland fans with a photograph of Bradley Lowery. Police said a 14-year-old had handed himself in and would be spoken to in due course. Coventry City said it was investigating and would cooperate with authorities.

segments.title: The family’s response
segments.body: Bradley died aged six from neuroblastoma in 2017. His mother, Gemma Lowery, said it was heartbreaking to see a favourite photograph used cruelly and asked that her son be remembered with love. She also said she did not want hatred directed at the fan.

content.headline: Skepta says immigration anger shaped his long-awaited new album
content.shortHeadline: Skepta’s new album confronts anti-immigrant rhetoric
content.standfirst: The Fork and Knife arrives after a long gestation, with Skepta describing a more reflective approach to his music and a desire to use his voice consciously. He discusses multicultural Britain, fatherhood and his past mistakes.

image.caption: Skepta, whose new album The Fork and Knife is due next week.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Ignorance towards immigration is horrible. It’s not British’: Skepta on his long-awaited return – and his anger at the racist right

segments.body: Skepta’s sixth album, The Fork and Knife, is due next week, almost three years after its announcement. The 15-track record moves between zouk-inflected R&B and grime, and pairs the veteran MC with younger artists. He says he wanted to make socially conscious music without losing its energy.

segments.title: A voice shaped by experience
segments.body: On “Innocent Smile”, featuring Madness frontman Suggs, Skepta attacks politicians’ scapegoating of immigrants and celebrates his parents’ journey from Nigeria to Tottenham. He connects that perspective to growing up around ska and skinhead culture in a mixed community, and calls current hostility to immigration “not British”.

segments.title: Learning from missteps
segments.body: Skepta also reflects on controversies he has apologised for, including artwork that unintentionally evoked the Holocaust and a Puma partnership he later regretted. He says the album’s long making process involved thinking about the consequences of his words, his own past errors and what rap might say beyond its familiar subjects.

content.headline: Radie Peat’s solo debut gives traditional songs startling force
content.shortHeadline: Radie Peat makes traditional songs feel newly urgent
content.standfirst: The Lankum singer’s first solo album gathers songs of female struggle, suffering and endurance. Peat’s spare arrangements and powerful voice make these familiar traditions feel immediate and unsettling.

image.caption: Radie Peat, whose solo debut reimagines traditional songs.

sources.originalTitle: Radie Peat: No Human Tongue Can Tell review – Lankum singer’s solo debut is the year’s best folk album

segments.body: No Human Tongue Can Tell opens with Peat singing “Hares on the Mountain” over restrained piano before Mellotron and Wurlitzer deepen the atmosphere. Across the album, she returns to traditional songs she has performed for years, letting their stories of women’s hardship and endurance emerge without ornamental excess.

segments.title: Songs that resist easy comfort
segments.body: Her reworking of “Willow Garden” becomes a haunted elegy, while “Still I Love Him” dwells on the painful bond between a woman and her abusive husband. Elsewhere, Liam Weldon’s “Dark Horse on the Wind” carries the weight of lost Irish republican hopes. John “Spud” Murphy’s production brings out the textures of breath, strings and percussion.

content.headline: Underscores turns a leap into pop into an arena-sized moment
content.shortHeadline: Underscores moves from online cult favourite to big stages
content.standfirst: After the acclaim for U and a support slot on Charli xcx’s tour, April Grey is adapting her ambitious hyperpop for larger venues. She talks about the album’s love songs, her shyness and a changing idea of success.

image.caption: Underscores, the recording name of musician April Grey.

sources.originalTitle: Pop prodigy Underscores: ‘I don’t think Gen Z is a loveless generation’

segments.body: April Grey, who records as Underscores, says her third album U was a deliberate attempt to make a focused pop record after the sprawling concept of 2023’s Wallsocket. The response has taken her from upgraded headline dates to arenas supporting Charli xcx, bringing the new challenge of reshaping her show for very different-sized rooms.

segments.title: Writing toward intimacy
segments.body: Grey set out to write nine love songs, a subject she had previously found difficult because of her own discomfort with intimacy. She rejects the idea that Gen Z is loveless, while acknowledging that dating can feel frightening. Meeting childhood musical hero Skrillex and touring with Charli have also prompted her to confront her shyness as her career grows.

content.headline: Rotterdam squat-punks Bombstrap make a racket with purpose
content.shortHeadline: Bombstrap channel Rotterdam’s squat-punk energy
content.standfirst: Led by visual artist and performer Eva Kah, the Rotterdam band’s debut album Big Enemy fuses raw guitars and chopped-up rhythms with a confrontational DIY sensibility. This week’s listening picks also range from house to dream-pop.

image.caption: Eva Kah, singer and visual artist with Rotterdam band Bombstrap.

sources.originalTitle: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: Dutch squat-punks Bombstrap’s uncompromising racket

segments.body: Bombstrap draw on the communal life of Het Poortgebouw, a well-known squatted centre in Rotterdam, for a sound that the Guardian describes as noisy, theatrical and resistant to the city’s gentrification. Eva Kah’s performance is as forceful visually as it is vocally; Big Enemy leaves its rough-edged guitars and rhythms open to interpretation.

segments.title: More new tracks to hear
segments.body: The same selection ranges well beyond punk: Clementine Douglas offers dramatic vocal house on “So Precious”, DJ Heartstring bring breakbeat energy to “3am/4am”, and saxophonist Josh Johnson sets two melodic ideas against each other on “Jazz Chord Possession”. Waterbaby’s “Creek” closes the picks with a waltzing, wounded lullaby.

content.headline: Olivia Tremor Control’s final album turns absence into psychedelia
content.shortHeadline: Olivia Tremor Control’s long-awaited farewell is haunted
content.standfirst: Recorded largely before the deaths of founding members Bill Doss and Will Cullen Hart, The Same Place is the Elephant 6 band’s first album in 27 years. Its psychedelic pop and shadowed sound make the release feel both intimate and uncanny.

sources.originalTitle: The Same Place

segments.body: The Same Place began taking shape in 2010, and most of it was recorded before Bill Doss died in 2012. The band added finishing touches after Will Cullen Hart died in 2024. Its songs return to Olivia Tremor Control’s mix of melodic pop and tape-loop experimentation, but the album’s long gestation gives its preoccupations with time and mortality a particular poignancy.

segments.title: Familiar sounds, darker shadows
segments.body: The record moves from the buoyant “Timewaster” to the unsettling “The Spinning Continuous” and the multipart “Path of the Parallels”. The review hears the band’s old hallmarks in the collage and pop instincts, while arguing that darkness now sits more persistently beneath the brightest moments.

content.headline: Heavensouls builds a vivid world from digital fragments
content.shortHeadline: Heavensouls finds beauty in a restless sound collage
content.standfirst: On the album-length EP cantu of the sower, 20-year-old producer Chidi Obialo combines free-jazz logic, strings and electronic detail. The result turns a lifetime of movement between physical and online worlds into an unsettled, often beautiful sound.

sources.originalTitle: cantu of the sower EP

segments.body: Recording as heavensouls, Chidi Obialo makes music from collisions: saxophone and strings sit among tiny digital sounds, samples and shifting rhythms. On the nearly nine-minute “today is my favorite”, layers swell and recede until a dense, restless construction finds a surprisingly serene close.

segments.title: A personal geography
segments.body: The EP draws on Obialo’s experience of moving from Nigeria, being unhoused for a time and later navigating the suburbs and online music worlds. Its samples include a call for liberation and a critique of capitalism, but the review also finds humour, anxiety and longing in the way the tracks keep changing shape.

content.headline: Susanne Sundfør’s church-recorded album demands full devotion
content.shortHeadline: Susanne Sundfør’s organ music leaves little room for doubt
content.standfirst: Revelations of Divine Love sets the Norwegian singer’s voice against pipe organ in a record inspired by the medieval mystic Julian of Norwich. Its austere commitment may feel transcendent or self-serious, the review argues, but it is difficult to meet halfway.

sources.originalTitle: Revelations of Divine Love

segments.body: Sundfør’s eighth album takes its title and subject from Julian of Norwich’s 14th-century devotional text. Recorded in a Norwegian church with organist Kit Downes, it relies almost entirely on pipe organ and Sundfør’s clear, steadfast voice, with repetition giving the music its meditative pulse.

segments.title: A demanding kind of stillness
segments.body: The review hears echoes of church music and Terry Riley’s minimalism, but finds the organ’s expressive range constricting across 13 tracks. That restraint can induce a trance, or settle into tedium. The album’s unwavering seriousness is its defining risk: listeners may find the devotion moving or off-putting, with little space for ambivalence.

content.headline: Mackeeper turn 2000s pop-rock nostalgia into sharp indie-pop
content.shortHeadline: Mackeeper’s playful pop exposes its own tricks
content.standfirst: Brothers Miles Cohen and Nick Harwood draw on aughts rock, radio pop and internet culture for their debut album Believe You Me. Its songs are carefully made and mischievously self-aware without losing their melodic pull.

sources.originalTitle: Believe You Me

segments.body: Mackeeper’s debut moves between crunchy guitar, pop hooks and rap-rock gestures, drawing on the sounds the New York siblings grew up with. “Men in Black” turns digi-rock swagger into a joke as well as a musical style, while “Vision” finds lead singer Miles Cohen in a sweeter, more earnest register.

segments.title: The joke has a hook
segments.body: The review’s pleasure comes from the tension between the duo’s polished songwriting and their knowing, sometimes irritating performance. On “Beautiful Stranger” and “Katie”, the songs seem to wink at their own catchiness, revealing pop’s tricks while remaining compelling examples of it.

content.headline: Romeo + Juliet made Shakespeare feel urgent to a new generation
content.shortHeadline: Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet still burns at 30
content.standfirst: Thirty years after its release, Baz Luhrmann’s maximalist adaptation still makes Shakespeare’s young lovers feel volatile and immediate. Leonardo DiCaprio and Claire Danes anchor a film whose style and soundtrack became part of its appeal.

image.caption: Claire Danes and Leonardo DiCaprio in Romeo + Juliet.

sources.originalTitle: Romeo + Juliet at 30: how Baz Luhrmann made teens fall in love with Shakespeare

segments.body: Luhrmann transposed the play’s feud to a sun-baked, media-saturated Verona Beach, retaining Shakespeare’s verse while surrounding it with gunfire, news footage and the rush of 1990s pop culture. The result drew criticism for its excess, but audiences came in large numbers and the film went on to earn more than $147m worldwide.

segments.title: A gateway to the Bard
segments.body: The Guardian credits the film’s feelings-first approach and its young leads with helping Shakespeare reach students who might otherwise resist the language. Claire Danes brings a particularly affecting freshness to Juliet, while the soundtrack—from Radiohead and Garbage to Des’ree—helped the film become a lasting point of reference for its generation.

content.headline: William Kentridge’s animated ballet finds black comedy in Soviet history
content.shortHeadline: Kentridge turns Shostakovich into a darkly comic ballet
content.standfirst: Oh to Believe in Another World pairs an animated collage with Shostakovich’s Tenth Symphony, performed live. The Guardian review finds a visually inventive work that holds grief and the absurdity of tyranny in the same frame.

image.caption: A scene from William Kentridge’s Oh to Believe in Another World.

sources.originalTitle: Oh to Believe in Another World review – William Kentridge’s amazing animated ballet of black comic pain

segments.body: William Kentridge’s hour-long cine-musical uses models, masks and live choreography to accompany Shostakovich’s Tenth Symphony. Stalin, Lenin, Trotsky and Mayakovsky appear as puppet-like figures moving through miniature Soviet settings that expand into uncanny, life-size worlds.

segments.title: A laugh edged with grief
segments.body: The review is struck by the work’s black comedy, especially the incongruity of Stalin’s monumental face above a dancer’s body. But Kentridge’s humour does not erase the horror: the film returns to lives destroyed by the state and to the longing for a better world that the symphony carries.

content.headline: Wicker’s unlikely romance sparks debate about desire and craft
content.shortHeadline: Wicker’s romance is both a gendered fantasy and a craft debate
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman’s Fisherwoman commissions a husband made of wicker, played by Alexander Skarsgård. Reviews and reporting on the film range from its provocative gender politics to questions about how convincingly its woven man is made.

image.caption: Olivia Colman’s Fisherwoman with the husband made for her from wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it
A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker
Basketweavers get in a twist over Alexander Skarsgård’s Wicker Husband

segments.body: The i Paper review calls Wicker a bawdy, funny and deliberately sexist fairy tale: the Fisherwoman’s new husband exists to please her, raising questions about agency and the fantasy of guaranteed devotion. The reviewer finds the film’s overcorrection against familiar gender roles both troubling and, in the end, oddly satisfying.

segments.title: Why the fantasy caught on
segments.body: The BBC reports that the trailer’s premise prompted an online wave of fascination with Skarsgård’s woven character. The filmmakers connect that appeal to domestic labour and the desire for a partner who notices what needs doing; a cultural critic also places the film within a longer tradition of romances between women and monstrous or unconventional men.

segments.title: A material question
segments.body: The Guardian’s reporting finds basket makers debating whether the character deserves to be called wicker at all: some object that he is plaited rather than woven or made from willow. The effects team says real willow could not meet the costume’s practical demands, so Skarsgård’s body was created from interlocking, specially printed pieces.

perspectives.body: Basket makers disagree over whether “wicker” names a material or a kind of weave. One maker says the costume is not how he would have approached the craft, while welcoming the attention the film has brought to endangered basket-making skills.

content.headline: Gentle Monster asks what loyalty means when a husband is accused
content.shortHeadline: Gentle Monster watches two women confront the men they love
content.standfirst: Marie Kreutzer’s drama follows a woman whose husband is investigated by police and a detective struggling to face her father’s behaviour. The review finds its strongest tension in the uncertainty neither woman can easily resolve.

image.caption: Léa Seydoux in Gentle Monster.

sources.originalTitle: Gentle Monster review – disquieting drama about two women facing the truth about the men they love

segments.body: Lucy, played by Léa Seydoux, leaves her life as an experimental musician to move to the countryside with her husband after his breakdown. When detective Elsa arrives with a search warrant, Lucy learns that her husband’s explanation for the police interest may not be true.

segments.title: The cost of denial
segments.body: The film parallels Lucy’s attempts to believe her husband with Elsa’s efforts to excuse her own father’s misconduct. Its central uncertainty concerns whether Lucy’s son may have been involved; although professionals find no evidence of abuse, the possibility remains unresolved. The review praises the two lead performances in this bleak study of loyalty and denial.

content.headline: Reviews disagree on whether The Social Reckoning can shake viewers
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning divides critics over its impact
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to The Social Network dramatises a whistleblower’s account of Facebook’s harms. One reviewer finds it a chilling mirror of everyday life; another says its drama lacks the tension to change anyone’s mind.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling
The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆

segments.body: The Social Reckoning centres on journalist Jeff Horwitz and former Facebook employee Frances Haugen, whose disclosures concerned the company’s recommendation systems, teen mental health and the spread of misinformation. In the i Paper review, the story’s movement from internal documents to the January 6 Capitol attack makes the film feel like a horror story about the viewer’s own online life.

segments.title: A less urgent reckoning
segments.body: The BBC’s review agrees that the film raises serious questions, citing its account of social media’s effects on teenagers, but finds the drama repetitive and low in suspense. It argues that the film’s whistleblower-and-reporter story lacks the conflict and urgency of the investigative classics it evokes.

perspectives.body: The BBC critic sees the film’s central paradox as its failure to persuade: although it dramatises social media’s influence, its lack of tension and a minor, underwritten Zuckerberg make the argument feel unlikely to change viewers’ minds.

content.headline: Ten films find fear in places beyond the horror genre
content.shortHeadline: These films prove horror does not need monsters
content.standfirst: For Halloween, Guardian writers look beyond conventional horror for films that unsettle through violence, social cruelty, obsession and dread. Their choices range from The Hunchback of Notre Dame to Burning and 2001: A Space Odyssey.

image.caption: Mia McKenna-Bruce in How to Have Sex, one of the films in the selection.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I left shellshocked’: writers on their scariest non-horror movies

segments.body: The selection makes the case that terror can come from ordinary people and systems, not just supernatural threats. Writers recall the cruelty directed at Quasimodo in Disney’s The Hunchback of Notre Dame, the social menace of Lee Chang-dong’s Burning and the slow-building unease of David Fincher’s Zodiac.

segments.title: Dread in different forms
segments.body: Other picks include the adolescent vulnerability of How to Have Sex, the institutional pressure in Dark Waters and the accumulated despair of Requiem for a Dream. Each contributor makes a personal case for the scene, image or human behaviour that stayed with them.

content.headline: Awkwafina returns to her family’s restaurant story in The Unlikely Cook
content.shortHeadline: Awkwafina turns her family’s restaurant history into TV
content.standfirst: Nora Lum travels across the US to learn from Asian American chefs and consider reviving her family’s closed Cantonese restaurant. She tells the Guardian how the series became a portrait of her grandmother and the family history behind the food.

image.caption: Awkwafina, whose series follows her family’s restaurant story.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I felt bad for my exes’: Awkwafina on making deeply personal TV – with her grandma

segments.body: In Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook, Lum visits chefs around the US as she explores whether she can bring her family’s restaurant back to life. Her great-grandfather opened Lum’s in Queens in the 1950s; the restaurant helped popularise Chinese-American dishes before closing in 1982, before Lum was born.

segments.title: A family story on camera
segments.body: Lum describes the series as a love letter to her grandmother, who helped raise her after her mother died when she was four. Filming together brought them into close conversation about the restaurant and its possible menu. Lum says her grandmother’s business later failed, costing her grandparents their home as well as their restaurant.

segments.title: What the food carries
segments.body: Lum says the series did not set out as a political statement, but that Chinese-American food cannot be separated from immigrant experience. She is still considering whether to reopen Lum’s, describing the possibility as a chance to give back and make her family proud.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family to a new legal drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up widens the world of the family-law drama
content.standfirst: Ritu Arya leads a Manchester-set spin-off with a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Its makers say the series keeps the family betrayals and romantic entanglements of The Split while telling a different family’s story.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up, with original series creator Abi Morgan.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The six-part drama follows Aria Kishan, a barrister expected to take over her family’s firm until her father changes his succession plans. A former love interest joins the practice, while her siblings and the family’s grief over their mother add complications of their own.

segments.title: Representation as ordinary life
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to portray British Asian characters living ordinary lives rather than confining them to a narrow set of familiar storylines. Original series creator Abi Morgan remains involved as an executive producer, supporting a new writing team as it carries forward the franchise’s themes of love, family and ambition.

content.headline: Matthew Perry documentary revisits a story he already told himself
content.shortHeadline: A new Matthew Perry documentary raises questions of dignity
content.standfirst: The One About Matthew Perry draws on archive and testimony from people close to the actor. The i Paper review finds it moving in places, but questions whether its intimate scenes offer insight or simply expose his loved ones’ grief.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Matthew Perry documentary is undignified and intrusive

segments.body: Netflix’s three-part documentary follows Perry from aspiring actor to Friends star and addiction campaigner, before his death in 2023. His sister and others describe the generosity and humour they remember alongside the addiction that shaped much of his life.

segments.title: What more can be told?
segments.body: The review notes that Perry’s 2022 memoir had already described his addiction in detail. It finds the documentary’s account of his death and the people who supplied him ketamine cursory, while objecting to long scenes of relatives recounting the moment they learned he had died. The critic argues that his own words and acting work remain the more respectful record.

content.headline: Laura Main reflects on Call the Midwife’s pause and caring for her mother
content.shortHeadline: Laura Main on Call the Midwife’s break and life off set
content.standfirst: With Call the Midwife taking a break before its next series, Laura Main is caring for her mother and performing in a play about Elizabeth II. She discusses the show’s future, her long relationship with Shelagh and the realities of unpaid care.

image.caption: Laura Main, who plays Shelagh in Call the Midwife and is appearing in By Royal Appointment.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I wanted my Call the Midwife character to age normally – even if I didn’t want to’

segments.body: Main has played Shelagh since Call the Midwife began in 2012, but did not film the programme this year. The BBC has confirmed a sixteenth series and a film, while a Christmas prequel, Sisters in Arms, is due to take the show’s place in the festive schedule.

segments.title: Care beyond the camera
segments.body: During the pause, Main has been helping care for her 91-year-old mother in Aberdeen while touring in By Royal Appointment. She says the experience has made her think about the pressures on unpaid carers and the difficulty many face in securing support. She also reflects on letting Shelagh age naturally over the show’s long run.

content.headline: November’s television slate ranges from Muhammad Ali to Blade Runner
content.shortHeadline: November TV: Muhammad Ali, Black Doves and Blade Runner
content.standfirst: BBC Culture’s monthly guide spans a drama about Muhammad Ali’s early years, a new season of Black Doves and a Blade Runner spin-off. It also flags returning favourites and several new comedies and crime stories.

sources.originalTitle: The Greatest to Blade Runner 2099: 12 of the best TV shows to watch this November

segments.body: Among the month’s headline arrivals is The Greatest, a drama following Muhammad Ali from childhood through the 1964 fight that made him world champion. The guide notes the involvement of Ali’s family and says the series aims to explore the path to fame as well as his boxing career.

segments.title: Returning worlds and new stories
segments.body: Other picks include the second season of Black Doves, with Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw returning to its spy-thriller world, and Blade Runner 2099, which imagines a future in which replicants hunt humans. The list also includes the latest seasons of The Gilded Age, Stick and Blue Lights, alongside newer comedies and dramas.

content.headline: Lara Croft at 30: the missteps behind a lasting game icon
content.shortHeadline: Lara Croft at 30: a legacy of hits and misfires
content.standfirst: The Tomb Raider heroine has survived annualised releases, awkward reinventions and marketing that often misunderstood her appeal. A birthday retrospective revisits those failures as well as the qualities that kept Lara Croft at the centre of gaming culture.

image.caption: Lara Croft in Tomb Raider IV–VI Remastered.

sources.originalTitle: Lara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blunders

segments.body: Thirty years after her debut, Lara Croft remains a gaming icon with more than 100 million Tomb Raider games sold. The Guardian’s retrospective looks at the less celebrated chapters: rushed annual sequels, the buggy and gloomy Angel of Darkness, and side characters who undercut the original games’ solitary sense of exploration.

segments.title: A character reduced and reclaimed
segments.body: The article also criticises marketing that sexualised Croft and a 2013 reboot that framed her suffering as a reason for players to protect her. It argues that her endurance owes more to the original games’ playability and her enigmatic independence than to the image imposed on her by developers and advertisers.

content.headline: After decades of playing games, a GamesMaster host enters one
content.shortHeadline: After 50 years of gaming, Greg Diamond gets in the game
content.standfirst: The Guardian writer voices a sailor in indie survival horror Black Tides Draga’s Wake. His account moves from the oddness of recording fight noises in a Nova Scotia garage to the joy of letting his children discover his performance for themselves.

image.caption: Draga, the protagonist of Black Tides Draga’s Wake.

sources.originalTitle: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one

segments.body: Greg Diamond’s first voice-acting role is the title character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake, a survival-horror game set aboard a decaying steamship. He describes learning to lower his voice to suit the character and improvising fight sounds for a team of developers working remotely in their spare time.

segments.title: A different kind of game bond
segments.body: Diamond connects the project’s small-team energy with the bedroom-programming culture of the ZX Spectrum era. His most affecting moment came when he played clips for his children without telling them he was involved and watched them recognise their father in the on-screen hero.

content.headline: Replaying Modern Warfare 2 with his adult son brings a father to tears
content.shortHeadline: A father and son revisit the game that started it all
content.standfirst: The Guardian writer and his 22-year-old son return to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the first game they played together. Their co-op failures and eventual teamwork become a reflection on parenthood, time and the pleasure of simply playing.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game father and son played together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The pair revisit Special Ops missions they first tried when the son was five. This time, they gradually learn to play together: the father advances cautiously and snipes from a distance, while his son charges ahead. They finally beat levels that had defeated them years before.

segments.title: A little more time together
segments.body: The writer describes the sessions as a rare return to carefree gaming, with food, late nights and room for repeated failure. The time is temporary: he and his son expect to move to different parts of the world within months. His son says he will remember these weeks as some of their best times together.

content.headline: Pompeii wardrobe yields a child’s charm necklace and everyday treasures
content.shortHeadline: Pompeii wardrobe reveals a child’s charm necklace
content.standfirst: A cabinet sealed by Vesuvius’s eruption held coins, cosmetics and personal belongings, including a necklace traditionally worn by children. The find offers a rare glimpse of everyday life in the Roman city.

image.caption: Personal belongings recovered from a home in Pompeii.

sources.originalTitle: Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe

segments.body: Archaeologists found a wooden wardrobe in a home on Pompeii’s Via dell’Abbondanza, containing items including tweezers, a perfume bottle, an incense burner and 38 bronze coins. Among them was a child’s necklace with more than 20 charms depicting deities including Bes and Mercury.

segments.title: What the objects suggest
segments.body: The necklace, known as a crepundia, was worn by children; its rattling charms could help parents keep track of them or identify them. Pompeii archaeological park director Gabriel Zuchtriegel said the objects may have belonged to people forced to flee suddenly, though that remains an interpretation.

content.headline: Manx shearwaters’ internal clocks can throw migrating birds off course
content.shortHeadline: Birds’ body clocks can disrupt migration navigation
content.standfirst: Analysis of two decades of tracking data suggests that eastbound Manx shearwaters can lose their bearings when their body clocks fall out of step with local time. The impact may be greater for inexperienced birds.

image.caption: A Manx shearwater, a seabird that navigates using the sun.

sources.originalTitle: Migrating seabirds face a surprising problem: jet lag

segments.body: Manx shearwaters use the sun as a compass, adjusting their direction according to its position and their internal clock. Researchers analysing 20 years of GPS data found that eastward flights across longitudes can leave the birds’ clocks about an hour behind local time, contributing to navigation errors.

segments.title: Experience matters
segments.body: The estimated effect on adults was modest: they corrected course, adding about 5km to a 1,000km journey. First-time foragers may lack the experience or map sense to recover, and could stray hundreds of kilometres. Richard Holland of Bangor University, who was not involved, called the finding significant but said the study does not establish what consequences the errors have for birds that return to their colonies.

content.headline: Venice lagoon was dry land as seas reshaped the northern Adriatic
content.shortHeadline: Venice lagoon was once dry land, study finds
content.standfirst: Researchers reconstructed 10,000 years of changing landscapes across the northern Adriatic. Their findings suggest the land now beneath the Venice lagoon once extended more than 30 miles from the coast.

image.caption: A canal in Venice, in a lagoon that researchers say was once dry land.

sources.originalTitle: How rising seas transformed dry land into Venice lagoon

segments.body: Researchers combined seismic data and sediment cores from coastal basins in Italy, Slovenia and northern Croatia to model changes in sea level. They conclude that the present-day Venice lagoon was once dry land, while Trieste was an area of hills overlooking swamps and lagoons.

segments.title: A changing coastline
segments.body: Sea levels rose in fits and starts beginning just over 10,000 years ago, at times by as much as 25mm a year. The researchers say Mesolithic hunter-gatherers had to adapt their hunting and fishing as the landscape changed; relative stability over the past 6,000 years helped settlements and farming develop.

content.headline: Vascular dementia may be overlooked; early blood-pressure care could help
content.shortHeadline: Vascular dementia may be more common than recognised
content.standfirst: Researchers and clinicians say vascular damage can be missed, including when it occurs alongside Alzheimer’s. Existing measures such as controlling blood pressure may reduce the risk of progression, but proposed drug treatments are still being tested.

sources.originalTitle: The little-known blood pressure pill benefits that could be dementia game-changer

segments.body: Vascular dementia is usually estimated to account for 20–30% of cases, but it may be under-recognised, particularly when it occurs alongside Alzheimer’s disease. Researchers describe links between damage to small blood vessels and the build-up of proteins associated with Alzheimer’s, complicating the distinction between the conditions.

segments.title: Prevention and possible treatments
segments.body: The article reports that blood-pressure drugs have been associated with fewer dementia diagnoses and that specialists advise attention to vascular health when memory problems are mild. Two drugs already used for chest or leg pain are being tested in UK trials for vascular dementia; whether they work remains to be seen.

content.headline: UK flu season starts early, but that does not necessarily mean a worse year
content.shortHeadline: Early flu season is a warning to stay alert, not a forecast
content.standfirst: UK flu infections are rising earlier than usual, with experts discussing viral changes and the timing of infections in the southern hemisphere as possible factors. Officials urge eligible people to get vaccinated, but the season’s eventual severity is uncertain.

sources.originalTitle: Why so many people are sick right now

segments.body: Flu activity in the UK has begun rising earlier than usual, though rates were still relatively low when the UK Health Security Agency reported the increase. Possible explanations include changes in circulating strains and a later flu season in Australia and other southern hemisphere countries; researchers have not established a single cause.

segments.title: What an early start can—and cannot—tell us
segments.body: An early season does not by itself predict a severe one: the previous year also started early and ended with fewer flu deaths than average. The UKHSA is urging people eligible for an NHS flu vaccine to take it up. Flu often begins more suddenly and causes more severe symptoms than a common cold, but symptoms alone do not settle every diagnosis.

content.headline: Longevity claims face scrutiny over age records, ‘Blue Zones’ and young blood
content.shortHeadline: A longevity researcher challenges popular anti-ageing claims
content.standfirst: Oxford demographer Saul Newman argues that weak age records and limited evidence undermine several celebrated longevity ideas. Those behind Blue Zones dispute his conclusions, and the piece also cautions that proposed anti-ageing effects of young-plasma transfusions are unproven.

image.caption: Oxford demographer Saul Newman, who has written critically about longevity research.

sources.originalTitle: I’m a longevity expert. These four anti-ageing myths are junk science

segments.body: Demographer Saul Newman argues that claims about people living to extreme ages can be undermined by poor records, and questions whether the regions branded “Blue Zones” have reliable evidence of exceptional longevity or distinctive diets. The account also describes commercial interests around Blue Zones; a spokesperson for the company behind the programme says its content is scientifically validated.

segments.title: Evidence and limits
segments.body: Newman also challenges the idea that telomere length offers a simple route to longer life and says there is no proven clinical benefit from transfusions of plasma from young donors to prevent ageing or memory loss. The article reports that Blue Zones’ proponents say his work has been debunked in peer-reviewed research; it does not resolve that dispute.

content.headline: Rising ADHD and autism diagnoses prompt warning, not proof of overdiagnosis
content.shortHeadline: Rising diagnoses raise questions about ADHD and autism
content.standfirst: A government-commissioned review says diagnosis rates for some young groups are approaching or exceeding estimates of how common the conditions are. It warns about possible overdiagnosis but says the evidence does not establish that it is happening at scale.

image.caption: Illustrative image accompanying reporting on ADHD and autism diagnoses.

sources.originalTitle: The four reasons why ADHD experts fear the UK is heading towards overdiagnosis

segments.body: The review found that NHS ADHD and autism diagnoses among children and young people are rising and, for some groups, approaching or exceeding estimated prevalence. It said the trend is a warning sign—not proof that overdiagnosis is already occurring at scale. Some families are waiting more than two years for assessments.

segments.title: Why assessment is difficult
segments.body: The report and experts cited in the article point to several possible contributors: diagnostic definitions have broadened, awareness has grown, and assessment relies on clinical judgements rather than blood tests or brain scans. The review also raises concerns about private assessment clinics and calls for regulation, while a psychiatrist notes that underdiagnosis and misdiagnosis can also occur.

content.headline: Binance resumes withdrawals after record crypto theft, says 95% of losses are: “
content.shortHeadline: Binance restarts withdrawals as it covers most stolen assets
content.standfirst: The exchange says it is restoring withdrawals in stages after the $6.3bn breach and has covered 95% of affected assets. The FBI attributes the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, though Binance says its investigation is not complete.

sources.originalTitle: Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion breach
Binance CEO says 90 percent of stolen assets have been ‘replenished’
North Korea linked to massive Binance crypto heist
Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history

segments.body: Binance says it has resumed withdrawals in phases, after freezing deposits and withdrawals following a theft it values at $6.3bn. The company says it has covered 95% of the stolen assets and will bear the financial impact rather than pass losses to users. Some withdrawals remain partly or fully suspended, and the exchange warns of delays.

segments.title: Attribution and open questions
segments.body: On Saturday, the FBI said a North Korean group it calls TraderTraitor was responsible and that it had observed the group converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum. Earlier reporting described a compromised engineer’s laptop as an initial lead, but Binance later said it had uncovered additional breach points. The company says it will publish a fuller incident report after its investigation.

perspectives.body: The FBI’s public notice attributes the theft to TraderTraitor and says it expects further laundering through decentralised finance and instant-swap services. The notice offered few other details or evidence.

content.headline: Investigation finds migrant workers face unsafe conditions on European data-cent
content.shortHeadline: Investigation finds abuses on European data-centre sites
content.standfirst: A cross-border investigation reports serious injuries, overcrowded housing, unpaid wages and safety concerns at data-centre construction sites. Contractors and technology companies say they have policies and procedures to protect workers.

image.caption: Illustration accompanying an investigation into conditions at European data-centre construction sites.

sources.originalTitle: Electrocutions, disease and no pay: how workers risk exploitation in Europe’s datacentres

segments.body: The Guardian and Investigate Europe report on migrant workers at data-centre sites in Sweden, Norway, Belgium and the Netherlands. One electrical tester described being badly injured in an arc-flash incident at a Google site in Belgium; hospital records reviewed by the outlets documented burns. The local labour inspectorate closed its investigation without finding wrongdoing, and no company or contractor appears to have been found liable.

segments.title: Housing, pay and oversight
segments.body: At a Microsoft site in Gävle, workers showed the outlets evidence of crowded accommodation and payslips that appeared to show long hours without overtime or holiday pay. A union says a settlement with subcontractor BenBau will provide back pay and allow union access. Google, Microsoft, BenBau and Collen say they require safe working conditions and compliance with relevant laws and standards.

content.headline: California ballot measure could fast-track projects—and data-centre reviews
content.shortHeadline: California measure raises concerns over data-centre oversight
content.standfirst: Proposition 45 would shorten environmental review timelines for eligible projects. Critics say its broadband language might let some data-centre developments qualify; supporters argue the measure would not apply to them.

sources.originalTitle: Prop 45 in California could be hiding a loophole for data centers

segments.body: California’s Proposition 45 would set deadlines for environmental reviews and legal challenges, limit the public-comment period and change how alternatives are considered. Environmental advocates and some legal experts warn that data-centre developers might try to qualify under the measure’s definition of essential broadband projects, potentially reducing public scrutiny.

segments.title: A disputed interpretation
segments.body: An attorney writing in the National Law Review argues that data centres’ role in supporting the internet does not make them essential broadband-access projects under the proposition. The measure’s supporters say faster reviews could help housing and clean-energy projects; the article reports no definitive ruling on how its provisions would apply to data centres.

content.headline: Court papers show Meta staff discussed a campaign to discredit Jonathan Haidt
content.shortHeadline: Meta staff discussed ways to undermine social-media critic
