content.standfirst: Meeting notes in a US legal filing describe a proposed “whisper strategy” against academic Jonathan Haidt, whose work has influenced debates over youth and social media. The documents do not establish whether Meta acted on the ideas.

image.caption: Academic Jonathan Haidt, whose work on social media and young people is discussed in the court filing.

sources.originalTitle: Meta discussed ‘whisper strategy’ against social media critic Jonathan Haidt, files show

segments.body: Internal meeting notes included in a US legal filing say Meta staff discussed how to get academics to disavow Jonathan Haidt, author of The Anxious Generation, and considered a “below-the-line” campaign. The notes predate the book’s publication and refer to a Substack post. It is not clear whether Meta put the ideas into practice.

segments.title: What the notes do—and don’t—show
segments.body: The document mentions a possible takedown piece by someone called “Gellman”. Statistician Andrew Gelman said he was never hired by Facebook to write a hit piece, though he had received money from Mark Zuckerberg’s company on a no-strings basis. Haidt said he was not surprised by the discussions; Meta had been approached for comment.

content.headline: Review links problematic digital-media use with risks to young people’s health
content.shortHeadline: Study links problematic media use to health risks for under-25s
content.standfirst: A Lancet series reviewing research on nine million people under 25 links problematic digital-media use with mental-health problems, sleep issues and less exercise. The researchers describe the associations as modest and not conclusive.

image.caption: Illustrative image accompanying research on digital-media use among young people.

sources.originalTitle: Three ways social media is harming young people, according to landmark study

segments.body: The review found that problematic digital-media use was associated with higher risks of mental-health problems, sleep difficulties and reduced physical activity among people under 25. Its authors called for coordinated action and urged technology companies to share platform data so researchers can investigate effects more independently.

segments.title: Calls for platform accountability
segments.body: The series chair said evidence linking problematic use to poorer outcomes is not conclusive, but justifies action. Researchers cited platform features such as infinite scroll, autoplay and personalised recommendations, and argued that companies should not place responsibility solely on users. The review does not establish that two hours of use causes harm.

content.headline: Why game remakes can bring back memories—and still disappoint fans
content.shortHeadline: Video-game remakes trade on nostalgia, but face a balancing act
content.standfirst: Players can return to familiar worlds with modern hardware and share them with new audiences. But nostalgia does not guarantee success: developers must balance the appeal of a classic with expectations for a fresh experience.

image.caption: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a classic game due for a remake.

sources.originalTitle: How video game remakes tap the power of nostalgia

segments.body: The article uses the planned remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time to examine how games can evoke memories through familiar places, music and learned skills. Researchers describe nostalgia as both pleasurable and tinged with loss, while the games industry sees remakes as a comparatively safe way to build on established audiences.

segments.title: The risks of returning
segments.body: Remakes can also frustrate fans if changes seem to displace the original or fail to meet high expectations. They can make older games easier to play on current hardware, but some players want new stories rather than revised classics. Analysts expect future remakes to rely more on reinterpretation or added content than on graphics alone.

content.headline: Open-source tool lets some Withings scale owners route health data elsewhere
content.shortHeadline: Open-source project offers a way around Withings sync fees
content.standfirst: YourOwnWeigh reroutes data from two older Withings scales to another server, allowing users to sync it to Apple Health without the company’s subscription. The project requires setup and does not yet support newer models.

sources.originalTitle: This open-source project lets you sync Withings data to other apps without a subscription

segments.body: Tom Anthony created YourOwnWeigh after Withings said new users would need a subscription to sync health data from its devices to third-party apps. The open-source project uses alternate firmware to send data from two older scale models to a server chosen by the user; Anthony says it can run on a free Cloudflare account.

segments.title: Compatibility is limited
segments.body: The project can import existing scale settings and profiles, and Anthony used Apple Shortcuts to move data from the alternate server into Apple Health. Support for other apps is a goal, not a current feature, and the tool is presently limited to two older scales.

content.headline: Startup’s new recycled-protein fibre receives first new US classification in 25
content.shortHeadline: New fibre classification turns textile waste into cashmere-like yarn
content.standfirst: Everbloom says its renoa fibre combines waste protein with a biodegradable biopolymer and has received a new classification from the US Federal Trade Commission. The startup is still scaling production, with its first product expected in 2027.

image.caption: A sample of Everbloom’s renoa fibre, presented as a cashmere-like material made partly from waste protein.

sources.originalTitle: Here’s what ‘renoa’ — the first new fiber in 25 years — feels like

segments.body: Everbloom says it makes renoa from waste protein, including scraps of cashmere and wool and down and feather lint, blended with a biodegradable biopolymer. The US Federal Trade Commission approved it as the first new fibre classification in 25 years, according to the company and the reporting.

segments.title: Still pre-market
segments.body: A TechCrunch reporter handled sample garments, including a scarf that the company said had been washed and tumble-dried repeatedly without shrinking or pilling. Everbloom is working with potential product partners; its first consumer product is expected in the second quarter of 2027. The account does not establish commercial-scale performance or environmental impact.

content.headline: Indigenous Australian artist warns AI imitations can strip cultural meaning
content.shortHeadline: Artist says AI imitations threaten Indigenous art and agency
content.standfirst: Pitjantjatjara artist Sally Scales says AI-generated work can appropriate First Nations art and cultural knowledge without permission or attribution. Advocates are calling for stronger control over how artists’ work and data are used.

image.caption: Pitjantjatjara artist Sally Scales, who says AI imitations can undermine artists’ agency and cultural knowledge.

sources.originalTitle: AI is stealing Indigenous Australian art and churning out ‘Temu slop’, artist says

segments.body: Sally Scales, chair of the National Gallery of Australia’s First Nations advisory group, says AI can imitate Indigenous art without the artist’s family lineage or lived experience, undermining both authorship and cultural meaning. Searches of online marketplaces found Aboriginal-style designs and products, often without attribution to an artist.

segments.title: Control and compensation
segments.body: The National Association for the Visual Arts says AI scraping can remove artists’ names and alter their work, while Indigenous data sovereignty includes authority over cultural material and knowledge. Intellectual-property specialists have proposed a framework requiring disclosure of training sources and giving creators more control; the Australian government says it is consulting on options for meaningful control and fair compensation.

content.headline: Judge allows NAACP lawsuit over xAI data-centre pollution to proceed
content.shortHeadline: NAACP pollution case against xAI can move forward
content.standfirst: A federal judge rejected xAI’s bid to dismiss a lawsuit alleging that turbines at its Colossus site near Memphis operated without required permits. The ruling allows the claims to proceed; it is not a finding that the company violated the law.

image.caption: The image accompanying reporting on the NAACP’s lawsuit over pollution at xAI’s Colossus site.

sources.originalTitle: Judge allows NAACP lawsuit over xAI data center pollution to move forward

segments.body: The NAACP, represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center, alleges xAI operated at least 35 combustion turbines and other pollution sources at its Colossus data centre without required air permits. xAI argued the turbines were mobile sources exempt from permitting and challenged the plaintiffs’ standing.

segments.title: The case continues
segments.body: Judge Debra M. Brown ruled that the plaintiffs have standing under the Clean Air Act and that the turbines are not mobile sources under Mississippi’s state plan. The decision rejects xAI’s motion to dismiss; it does not resolve the underlying allegations. The NAACP describes the ruling as an important step in its effort to hold the company accountable.

content.headline: Apple plans to bring some Apple Intelligence features to China in iOS 27.3
content.shortHeadline: Apple Intelligence features set for China, without new Siri
content.standfirst: An iOS 27.3 beta is expected to bring several existing Apple Intelligence tools to Chinese users, including translation and writing features. The announcement does not include Apple’s newer Siri AI.

sources.originalTitle: Apple Intelligence is finally coming to China with iOS 27.3

segments.body: Apple says an iOS 27.3 beta scheduled for November 4 will bring some Apple Intelligence features to China, with a full release planned for December. The initial offering includes notification summaries, translation, writing assistance, visual intelligence and tools to remove objects from photos.

segments.title: A limited first release
segments.body: The rollout does not include the newer Siri AI. Apple says it has worked with Alibaba to add support for its Qwen chatbot in some experiences. Reuters previously reported that Apple trained a language model specifically for China; the gathered report does not detail how each feature will work in practice.

content.headline: Sam Altman argues scarce RAM is better used in data centres than personal PCs
content.shortHeadline: Altman says cloud computing should get priority for scarce RAM
content.standfirst: OpenAI’s chief argues that shared data-centre memory is used more efficiently than RAM sitting idle in personal computers. The view comes as long-term supply deals for AI infrastructure add pressure to memory availability and prices.

sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk

segments.body: Sam Altman said on the Cheeky Pint podcast that, when memory is scarce, it is “quite terrible” for people to keep RAM in personal computers if they use it only a small fraction of the time. He argued that cloud systems can make better use of limited supply through higher utilisation.

segments.title: Who gets the supply?
segments.body: The report says memory makers Samsung and SK Hynix have long-term deals with cloud operators and projects such as OpenAI’s Stargate, reserving a substantial share of future RAM output. That competition may contribute to higher prices for consumer technology. Altman’s argument reflects OpenAI’s interest in securing capacity; it does not settle how memory should be allocated.

content.headline: OpenAI’s mathematical results stir debate over disclosure, verification and pace
content.shortHeadline: OpenAI’s math output leaves researchers weighing access and scrutiny
content.standfirst: Sam Altman says OpenAI will keep releasing AI-generated research results, despite researchers’ complaints about rushed communication and inadequate attribution. The company has also withheld details of one claimed breakthrough, citing expert advice.

sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman sympathizes with mathematicians, but says OpenAI’s math onslaught won’t stop

segments.body: Altman said he sympathises with mathematicians struggling to assess a stream of AI-generated results, but believes the public’s access to scientific knowledge outweighs the disruption. The Verge reports that OpenAI has released hundreds of mathematical results this month, often in brief write-ups that researchers have described as difficult to follow.

segments.title: Disclosure and verification
segments.body: Researchers have criticised the company over attribution, context and verification, saying they are left to check and interpret the claims. OpenAI has also kept details of a claimed result in Yang–Mills theory from public release, saying it followed recommendations from a hand-picked expert group. The reporting describes disagreement over that approach, not an independent assessment of the mathematical claims.
